txt: Reluctantly, she takes the pen from your hand, scribbles her name on the line, and hands everything back to you.
She keeps humming, nodding her head back and forth to her unknown melody.
She nods and raises her unseeing eyes. "What are you interested in then?"
She nods, rinsing another piece of cloth.
She waves her hand southwest. "Over there you can find... more of the same. Shacks and trees growing wild. That's the Pox."
The old woman shakes her head slowly. She drops the rag into the bucket -- it's clean now.
The old woman shakes her head slowly.
The old woman shrugs. "Or don't. It's your choice. No skin off my teeth."
The old woman still hums her unknown song. She opens her eyes to acknowledge your presence.
The old woman still sits in her chair, continuing with her chores. As she does so, she quietly hums to herself.
The woman next to a bucket of clothes hums an odd melody. Her eyes are closed.
"'Surrender to the Night'," she replies, slowly rocking back and forth.
"'This *shit*?" Her eyes with their cataracts look at you. "I'm not going to do your work for you, just because you've got a potty mouth."
"*Stay*? Most people here are trying to *leave*..."
"A deal with who?" She narrows her eyes, then scoffs. "It's the Débardeurs Union, isn't it?"
"A lullaby my mother used to sing. I sang it to my kids too. It's an old Samaran children's song."
"A radio? Hah -- no, we play no radio here. There is one in the shack, but it's never used."
"Adu hai indung suhoorang..."
"After the war it was turned into a goodwill hospital for shell-shocked veterans and folks looking for some quiet in the old sanatorium gardens."
"Ah, I should have known..." She shakes her head. "This is yet another Union mess. I'm not afraid of them, you know. We're not in the habit of being afraid around here."
"Ah, look at me ramble on." She waves her hand. "What brings you to us?"
"Although I guess she was pretty handy with the mechanical and technical stuff. Even fixed the heater in the shack. You should be thankful for that."
"An old military hospital and its surroundings." She looks toward the buildings to the south. "Or it used to be, during the time of the Suzerain."
"An uncomplicated man," she nods approvingly. "I take it that means you're interested?"
"And now *suspicious*-looking people are sneaking around the church. I don't like that."
"And now you know everything there is to know about this coast." She drops a bar of soap into the bucket with a splash.
"And then there's the drunks..." She sighs. "Not a pretty sight, but there's little we can do about it. Home is home, even for them."
"And what do you think I'm doing right now, Mr. RCM?!" The scrub brush flies into the bucket so furiously some splashes hit your face.
"Any day now." Her eyes turn to the sky. "I'm sure of it. Are you interested or not?"
"Anyhow, you might ask Lilienne if she's seen anything lately -- that girl's got a way of attracting lost and broken things."
"Anything else, now?" The old woman frowns. Her wrinkles frown with her.
"Anything else?" A cold breeze rushes by. The old woman smiles.
"Are you getting a reward for it at least?"
"Are you sure you wouldn't rather stay here, get a nice, cozy fire going in the heater?" She drops the rag into the bucket -- it's clean now. "Seems like a better idea to me..."
"As I said. It's a peninsula. There's no one there. Just ghosts and vagrants. And teenagers making out."
"As I've done before when she's been in trouble, or just looking for solitude. I've made it clear -- we welcome all kinds of people here."
"As you please."
"At least those who remain..." She falls silent and turns to look over her shoulder, as though looking for someone.
"Aye, even *I* can see that. I told you not to bring your trouble with you, policeman. We've got troubles of our own here..."
"Aye, laundry fetchers are some of the most *honourable* people I know." Her smile gleams like a freshly honed knife.
"Aye, officer. I certainly will."
"Aye, that you are, dark Omen -- help yourselves and your organization. Help the storm clouds gather on the horizon..." She shakes her head.
"Aye, they're good kids. I brought them up the right way." There's a touch of pride in her voice.
"Aye, we do... we do..." A hint of sadness passes through her face. "But how do we do that?"
"Aye. Lilienne's not the only one who's too trusting."
"Aye." Her eyes grow wide with glee. "Sometimes it's as though I've also gotten lost inside this nameless nothing."
"Aye." She nods and looks at the shack. "The room is pretty bare bones, but it's got a bed and roof over it. That's more than some folks have around here."
"Aye? Do tell." A seagull flies overhead -- obviously a bad omen.
"Aye? What's this about?" She takes out the documents and squints her eyes. "Come now, I can't read all this scribble. Tell me what it says."
"Because you're an *ill omen*. But you're still welcome here as long as men with guns aren't chasing you. And maybe even then, because that's the kind of fishing village we've built."
"Before you get to the church, there's some ruins -- an apartment complex, or some kind of electrical plant... Run down bunch of houses, empty."
"Bidjakla sana dipandang manis... "
"Change your mind, did you? I thought you might. Won't find a better deal than free."
"Cops bribing citizens? Doesn't it usually go the other way around?" She doesn't wait for your reply.
"Did you say something?" She squints at you.
"Do you know who takes the cream off these deals? Real estate developers, construction companies, restaurant owners, Claire's accountants in La Delta..."
"Don't make an old woman regret opening her house to the police." A key appears from under her apron. She hands it to you.
"Don't make this old women regret giving the police the key to her house." She takes out a key from under her apron and hands it to you. "Here."
"Exit from what?"
"Fine," she mutters. Grabbing a pen from inside her apron pocket, she scribbles her name on the dotted line and hands the document back to you.
"Get out of here, trying to ruin my day!" She raises her bony finger. "And that youth centre better be a good one or you'll have trouble from me."
"Go ahead," she remarks sharply, "call people rude things. We've heard worse here. Now are you interested or not?"
"God damn that girl," she murmurs softly.
"Gone and hid things in there..." She shakes her head. "She's usually a good tenant. And not a *stupid* one either."
"Good for you. Can't expect to receive help if you're not helpful in return. A fine arrangement, that."

"Hah!" She lifts the paper very close to her face and studies it intently. "I might be half blind, but it looks like part of the village is gonna be a street. The best part. The part we need to get out of our houses."
"Have some integrity. You're an officer of the law, not some fat slug's corrupt little crony."
"Have you asked Lilienne about this? I won't even consider signing till I know she's on board." She hands the envelope back.
"He did too many narcotics. So many he fell off his boat and split his skull on a buoy." She rubs soap off her hands. "Folks who saw it, say his head cracked open like a melon. Nasty-nasty."
"He probably pawned it for booze and then forgot about it. You know how drunk men are..."
"He was brooding, needed some help opening the door. You got it open for him and took him to think about what he'd done in a more secluded place. Somewhere more quiet."
"He's a sharp one," she says to herself and runs her hand across the washboard.
"Heh..." Not a muscle moves in the wrinkled face. "I'd like to see him try. If anything, *I* am gonna muscle *him* out with construction noise."
"Here? For you?" She lets out a dry chortle. "No, officer. The only money we have here is some coins the drunks tried hiding from their women -- and then forgot about."
"How would I know? She's a gruff one, but not violent. She doesn't go around toting a gun." She looks back toward her shack, thinking.
"I *can* wash it for you," she says after looking the jacket over, "but it's going to take about a half an hour. Think you can stay put for that long?"
"I can see that," she nods, a clever flicker in her eyes. "Everyone can see you think well of yourself. Now are you interested or not?"
"I cleaned it, like I always do."
"I don't believe that. Police showing up here, collecting signatures -- this has Union written all over it."
"I don't believe the fat man's *youth centre* is gonna change anything. But what other choice do we have? It's not like the Coalition Government is coming to save us..."
"I don't know exactly. A pre-war place. It used to be something." She shrugs. "Before the war. I wasn't here then, you know. Was born in Samara."
"I don't know... further up the coast. She tried to leave quietly but the hinges on that door screech like a cat in heat -- woke me up. I heard her rushing in those heavy boots, heading up north."
"I raised my own kids in this village and they're doing fine for themselves."
"I see Lilienne's name is already here. Tsk, tsk. The girl is too trusting. Either way, I won't sign Union papers." She hands the envelope back to you.
"I still have a golden ear. Come-come." She beckons you toward her.
"I told you before! No, there has been no listening to the radio. Not last week, not in the weeks before."
"I warned you," she nods solemnly. "I warned you men with guns would be coming after you. They always are with your kind..." Her features soften.
"I wield an army of drunks." A clever smile passes her face. "Do not underestimate the effect of such a force if it's pointed to the right direction."
"I won't be around much longer, anyway. Not with the dampness in my bones." She looks at her knees. "If they want to take a chance, who am I to stop them?"
"I won't be going anywhere." She side-eyes the bucket full of clothes.
"I won't charge you for it. Take it as a gesture of goodwill, from the village to the RCM."
"I'm not going anywhere." Her features soften. "Perhaps there's something else the village can do for you, huh? Though we don't have much here -- just garbage. And a skiff or two..."
"I'm not sure those were the last of the men with guns, either." She nods. "There are always more coming for your kind, officer."
"I'm sorry there's not a lot of room to park your motor carriage. And not a lot of houses. Or a lot of people. My kids are long gone... searching for treasure. So are others'."
"I'm sure you did," she says with a peculiar smile and nods. "Nature keeps them in rotation. A new face pops up every now and then and an old one disappears and is forgotten. This is who we are."

"I've heard that pitch before plenty. 'Building this, building that, new jobs, new blood...'" She shakes her head in disdain. "Somehow the people here always end up holding the short end of the stick."

"I've seen it all before. You think they've got *our* interests at heart? Rich men are always selling poor men promises they never plan to keep..." She pulls a dark red rag out of the bucket and puts it back.
"If you say it is," she says, shrugging.
"Is there anything else I can help you with?"
"Isn't that what people always think when they're lost?" A fleeting smirk runs across her lips. "Something *I* can do to help you find your way, officer?"
"It's okay," she calms you. "What matters is we are still around. Still living our lives. Even in 'pornographic' poverty we make do..."
"Just us." She sounds tired. "It's barely a village anymore. We... *almost* don't exist."
"Like I said," her tone sharpens, "it's an old *children's* song. You don't have to like it."
"Like a smart dog, yes?"
"Lilienne is tough." She nods. "Tougher than the men here at least. If it wasn't for her and the kids, this place wouldn't have a spark of life left."
"Lilienne should let her sword make her decisions. The girl just doesn't have the head for it." She lets out a chortle, coarse like a raven's caw. "Either way, I won't sign."
"Losing a family member's tough," she nods solemnly. "But we've all lost someone we're close to, some more than once."
"Maybe they're afraid."
"Maybe," she says with unnerving calm. "It would be easy. But right now you want something from me, right?"
"Me? No one. Just an old washerwoman. Mother called me Isobel, if that's what you're asking. And my married name is Sadie."

"Mhm, that's exactly how they get ya. That's why we built our own cinder block houses on the seaside. So we don't have to give money to those crooks..." She looks around. "They might not look like much, but they're *ours*."
"Must say, I'm proud of this one," she nods, handing the jacket back to you. "It's pretty nice underneath all that filth. I hope it'll have an easier life in your hands."
"Must say, I'm proud of this one," she nods, handing the jacket back to you. "It's pretty nice underneath all that filth. I hope you take better care of it than its last owner."
"My kids grew up and left, like they do. The house is long empty now. I live in the small side attachment -- it's easier and cheaper to keep warm."
"My suggestion is -- don't. Don't grow any older than you already are. That's old enough." She smiles. "What's troubling your mind?"
"Nay, I haven't *seen* anyone lately."
"No one is using it and god knows it's not much anyway." She tilts her head on the side, pondering over something. "You can stay there."
"No one, that's why it's closed." After a long pause, she adds, "It was once a bustling place, back when I was young and so was everyone else..."
"No! They're good kids. I brought them up the right way." There's a note of defiance in her voice.
"No, I have no idea where they heard it. They've been in earshot all week, and no radio."
"No, it's *not* like that man. With him, we called you. Right now, you just arrived by yourself. Like a raven, plucking at the window glass."
"No, not you personally. I meant the RCM. Some of the men got into a fight, one of them killed another. Locked himself in that woodshed over there," she points to the building behind her.
"No, she was mostly silent this time. Kept to herself..."
"No, you're not. I've seen you around here before. Twelve years ago. You didn't raise any hell -- you were quite helpful, actually. But, still, in Martinaise you're considered an ill omen."
"No. They've tried, but things just keep happening. Crime. *Accidents*. Other things. The place never stays open." She frowns. "It's a pity. It used to be such a nice church."
"No..." She tilts her head to the side, looking up at you, deep in thought. "She's a fighter."
"No..." the old woman says, her cloudy eyes darting sideways. "They moved to Faubourg for work."
"No."
"None of my business, either way. How you spend your hours is up to you..."
"Not much..." She replies and wipes her forehead. "There's the abandoned church -- the Dolorian Church of Humanity. It's been there since before my time even."
"Not that I know of, though she was into nice music. She once showed me a few mixtape-milieus she'd made." She brushes her forehead with the back of her hand. Water drips to the ground.
"Nothing good ever comes from paperwork, in my experience." She nods.
"Nothing of the sort." She shakes her head. "Sure, she was no stranger to the bottle... she fit in, that way. But I only knew her to have a beer on the beach while watching the sunset..."
"Now it's your turn, mister...?"
"Now the area is criss-crossed with nameless streets and makeshift cinderblock houses. Shacks as far as the eye can see."
"Now what catch we *do* bring in goes straight into a lorry for the Delta or somewhere else."
"Of note? The old fishmarket up on the boardwalk. But it's closed."
"Oh, aye, must be *real* important from the sound of it..."
"Oh, of course. Last time we saw you around here was... twelve years ago. You also came to take care of trouble then. Which you *did*... but, still, in Martinaise you're considered an ill omen."
"Oh, the usual. Dark tidings. Black hound."
"Oh." A shadow passes over her face. "Welcome, police officer. We don't cause any trouble around here -- and we don't *want* any trouble either."
"Oh?" Her expression betrays curiosity. "It seems to be a common theme these days."
"One thing. Officer, if you do find her, please go easy on her..." She looks around. The air is getting colder.
"Our tenant, the policeman. I hope the waves don't keep you up at night. What can I help you with?"
"Quite a handle you got there." The old woman nods, with evident respect. "So many titles. One of them *double*."
"Save your breath, officer. This deal isn't going anywhere. Now if you'll excuse me, I've got this whole bucket-full of rags to finish. That's my job. Maybe you should do yours?"
"See that you didn't just get us all screwed. I might be half-blind, but I have a good memory for treachery."
"She came last Friday. Left on Monday, in a hurry..." Her wrinkled hand kneads a blue rag in the water. "What has she gotten herself into, that girl?"
"She isn't what you'd call a *drunk*. Even offered me some, from time to time. Said it was part of the camionneur life. But I never saw her lose control of herself, the way some people do."
"She tried not to let it show, but I could tell she hadn't come to fish -- usually she likes to cast a few lines, but this time she mostly stayed in her room."
"She's a good girl, whatever she's gotten herself mixed up in."
"She's good company. Knows how to talk to an old woman." She rubs her cold hands together. "At my age, you don't get a lot of quality conversation, so I really appreciate that about her."
"She's right over there." She points towards the jetty. "The dark-haired woman, leaning over the railing."
"So be careful. And don't be a hero."
"Some things just don't *fly*, officer." She smiles a gap-toothed smile and smells the air. "Look around. Who'd go to church here? They built it three hundred years ago, must have been nicer then..."
"Sooner or later you'll see for yourself." She slowly shakes her head. "Don't have to look long to find these guys."
"Still, I'm sorry to hear about your partner. He seemed to be a decent enough sort."
"Suit yourself," replies the old woman and shrugs. "Patience obviously isn't your strong suit."
"Suit yourself," she says, tucking some loose hair back under her shawl. "But should you ever need shelter, remember old Isobel and her shack by the sea."
"Suliram yang manis..."
"Suliram, suliram, ram, ram..."
"Surely not the first one..." She looks you over, a clever smile on her lips. "So are you interested or not?"
"That bad, is it?"
"That doesn't mean you're wrong though," she sighs. "This place ain't what it used to be, even I can see that..."
"That said, if lodgings is what you're looking for, I've got a free room in the shack." Her soapy thumb points to the building behind her.
"That the best you can say about your *partner*? Sounds like it wasn't working out."

"The Ecclesiastes have tried to get things going there, but things just keep happening. Crime. *Accidents*. Other things. The place never stays open." She frowns. "It's a pity. It used to be such a nice church."
"The good will ran out." She tightens the scarf around her neck. "The staff left and the place was shut down. It's long gone by now."
"The lack of wealth is the one thing we've got in abundance." The woman smiles cryptically.
"The policeman." She squints at you. "What can our village do for you?"
"Then all's not lost," she replies, smoothing a wrinkle in her skirt. "As you can see, even in 'pornographic' poverty people make do..."
"Then the poor get pushed out of their homes and the rich get a little richer. That's the way it goes. So no, I don't trust the fat man, and neither should you."
"Then..." the old woman exhales. She stares at the ground, unable to finish the thought.
"There's not much *to* tell. People come and go. Now, was there something else?"
"These ears know every sound that belongs to this coast. I would know if I heard anything different."
"These things happen occasionally. Don't worry, you'll find yourself once more."
"This is my little cinderblock town." She nods with a wrinkled smile. "I know what goes on around here."
"This is pretty much a non-place." She grins. "A gap. A blank spot on the map, just a cluster of nameless shacks on a nameless street."
"Though I suppose you took the worst of it. Turns out you were your *own* ill omen." The woman chuckles to herself.
"Thought so." The old woman inhales sharply. "So what do the Claire brothers want this time?"
"Tut, tut. Don't be shy now. It's going to be alright."
"Used to be a supply depot... we think. Sending goods and ammo across the bay. It's jammed shut, though. We tried to get in, see if there was anything to sell or scavenge, but it's impossible."
"Was that the nonsense they were spouting? Pah!" She shakes her head.
"Welcome to the fishing village." She opens her eyes. "Please lean in closer. I have cataracts."
"Well, I imagine they'll grow up and leave, too."
"Well, hand it over then and I'll see what I can do..."
"Well, there's Lilienne and her kids. A few new folks live in the house to the east." She nods her head across the courtyard. "But they're away right now."
"Well, there's that music. Music from across the sea." She scoffs. "It started a few days ago and now it's blasting, even through the nights."
"Were you dropped on the head as a kid? You can't live off a pittance for long..."
"What do you expect? Police officers get put into dangerous situations all the time. Sometimes they get shot. It's a rough trade you're in."
"What do you mean, 'what's going to happen'? They're gonna grow up, of course..."
"What do you want with a lost jacket?"
"What kind of foolishness is that? A cop's got to have a partner. That's in your nature, however you may deny it."
"What more do you want to know about that poor girl?"
"What you'll find is poverty and abandon." She grins. "Not much of a threat you've got there."
"What, you're one of those real-estate people with big plans? If you want a development opportunity, you can check out the abandoned building over at Land's End."
"What? You're fetching someone's missing laundry *free of charge*? Do you not have anything better to do?"
"Why would I do that? That's a fool's name. Are you a fool?" Her bony finger raises before you can speak. "Don't ridicule yourself before an old woman, officer. It's undignified."
"Why, I guess I will, Harry. Aye, it just rolls off the tongue. I used to know a Harry. Strong lad, but dumb as a rock."
"Would you now?" She turns to him. "I know how this world works, and it doesn't work when people tell on each other."
"Wouldn't *dance* with you? Is that what you look for in a partner?"
"Yes, early, with the dogs -- around 8 o'clock, I think."
"Yes, it's going to be too much work for you to find her." She drops the rag into the bucket -- it's clean now. "Better for you to stay here, get a nice, cosy fire going in the heater..."
"Yes, let's hear those other questions." She looks around as spring snow starts falling -- lightly on the fishing village.
"Yes," she replies, slowly nodding. "You do that. Can't let fat Mr. Claire down now, can you?"
"Yes. I can't really sleep anymore. Only a few hours a night. It happens when you grow older..." She sloshes the water in the bucket around for a bit.
"Yes." She nods. "It does."
"You best not be plotting another revolution under my roof," she mumbles. "We barely got through the last one... But the room -- do you want it?"
"You need to check your facts, officer." Her bony finger is pointing at you, soapy water dripping on the skirt. "I said no such thing."
"You watch your tongue, boy. This village has held up much better than *some* people." Even with her cataracts she can pierce right through you.
"You'll never find her, you know." Her tone is without malice. "She knows the coast like the back of her hand. *You* only just arrived."
"You're still welcome here." She nods. "As long as men with guns aren't chasing you. And maybe even then, because that's the kind of fishing village we've built."
"You're trying to wink at me, aren't you? I can't see, or did you forget that part?"
"Your mind just flips back and forth, doesn't it... what are they about *exactly*?"
"Your parents must have had big plans for you." She pauses, measuring you up and down. "Wonder if you measured up?"
“Yes, I let my room to that Ruby girl…” She speaks slowly, wringing out a rag, after a long silence. Her hands move into the water bucket. Some water sloshes over the edge.
